newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian pension fund investments to be liberalised.
newsitem.headline: Belgian pension fund investments to be liberalised.

text.p: A rule obliging Belgian pension funds to hold "at least" 15 percent of their assets in Belgian government debt will be scrapped under a new law presently under preparation, an official source told Reuters on Thursday.
"This will be done away with," the source said.
A spokesman for the regulatory Insurance Control Office declined to comment. He confirmed, however, work was under way to revise the 1985 law which presently limits the sector's investments.

"At this point in time pension funds don't have the same freedom to invest as insurance companies. There will be some kind of alignment, although this does not mean that they will be identical," the spokesman said.

Chris Verhaegen, director of the Belgian Pension Fund Association, said in practice a change in the law, which was designed at a time when the Belgian bond market was not well developed, will not make much difference to funds' holdings.
In 1995, the last year for which figures are available, Belgian pension funds invested 33.2 percent of their 234 billion francs of assets in Belgian bonds, well above the statutory minimum.
Verhaegen said the Association would reserve judgment on any change in the law until a full draft had been published.
"From the contacts we have had we know the rules will be more flexible in certain areas, but they could be more restrictive in others," Verhaegen said.

Belgium moved to scrap restrictions on investments by insurance companies in 1994. A rule that obliged insurance companies to also hold at least 15 percent of their technical reserves in government paper was done away with along with other rules limiting investments to mainly Belgian franc denominated assets.
However, the 1985 law that governs Belgian pension funds retains the 15 percent government debt requirement. Investment in overseas property is also banned.
